newsitem.title: JAPAN: FEATURE - Japan awakens to electronic cash potential.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Japan awakens to electronic cash potential.

text.p: Japanese consumers may be happy to let wads of cash burn holes in their pockets, but bureaucrats, bankers and the phone company are waking up to the potential of replacing those bills and coins with electronic money.

Banks, worried they might lose a key chunk of their core payment business to non-financial rivals such as software companies and network providers, are weighing options to stay in the game when electronic cash catches on.
The trade and telecommunications ministries are jostling for funds to promote new business and technologies, and regulators are pondering potential legal hurdles and monetary policy fallout.
"It is likely that electronic fund transfer and electronic money will spread more quickly in Japan than was originally thought," said a Yamaichi Research Institute report.
Just how and when that will happen remains to be seen.
The concept of electronic cash covers a wide range of new payment systems now being developed around the world.

Experts speak of two broad types -- those using "smart cards" to store value on a computer memory chip and transfer it via special card-readers, and those transferring value as "cybermoney" through a computer network like the Internet.

Such distinctions, however, are blurring as systems emerge combining "smart cards" with networks, while some predict "smart cards" will evolve to combine credit functions for larger purchases and electronic cash for smaller payments.
Japanese banks appear to view the dawning of an electronic cash era with considerable concern and a modicum of enthusiasm.

"If banks don't get involved and firms from other industries such as software or network providers do, banks will lose their key payment business," said Tetsuhiko Saito, a manager at Fuji Bank Ltd's multimedia business division.
"So we want to defend that business while also attacking new business opportunities," he told Reuters.

Sakura Bank Ltd says banks have little choice but to join the fray. "Banks feel a sense of crisis over the possible rapid spread of electronic money," Koichi Ishida, Sakura's assistant general manager for electronic network business development, told Reuters. "By getting involved, we are trying to protect part of our main business."

Sakura and Fuji, along with other rival banks, are participating in a number of electronic cash and credit projects, some sponsored by the Ministry of International Trade and Industry (MITI) and involving either Visa International or MasterCard International and Japanese credit card companies.
MINISTRY WANTS TO ENCOURAGE ELECTRONIC COMMERCE

MITI wants to promote electronic cash and credit as part of its push to encourage electronic commerce -- commercial transactions and payments over computer networks -- which it sees as a way to develop new businesses and technologies.
The Trade Ministry earmarked 31.75 billion yen ($288 million) funds for its Electronic Commerce project in the year to March 1996.

Among the projects sponsored by MITI are "Smart Commerce", involving Visa and Toshiba Corp, and the "UC Settlement Project", involving MasterCard, Japan's UC Card credit card firm and electronics companies Hitachi Ltd and Fujitsu Ltd.
Six banks including Fuji, Sakura and Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd are also official observers in an electronic money project planned by the Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications (MPT).

MPT, which secured 1.7 billion yen ($15.4 million) in 1995/96 to fund electronic commerce projects, wants additional funds next business year to start a three-year test of an electronic cash concept developed by domestic telecoms giant Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp (NTT), a ministry official said.

NTT applied on September 10 for patents for the system, developed with help from a Bank of Japan think tank. NTT's experimental system stores electronic cash on an IC card and allows transfer at shops or over a network like the Internet.

The telecoms ministry official said it was too early to say who would use NTT's system, but banks worry it might give a competitive edge to the giant postal savings system or "Yucho". "It's great to develop telecoms technology, but if Yucho, which is basically a bank that can't go bankrupt, gets involved in electronic money, banks would not be able to compete and are naturally upset about that," said one financial source.

Industry experts say banks, many of which have been engrossed in cleaning up their non-performing asset troubles, are not uniformly enthusiastic about electronic money. "Some are keen and some are not," said a Finance Ministry official.
Given uncertainty over which type of electronic cash will catch on worldwide, banks want to keep their options open, said Yamaichi Research analyst Kazuyuki Tone.
Sakura's Ishida says his bank is still keen on Mondex, the brainchild of Britain's National Westminster Bank.

The Mondex system stores money on a "smart card" computer chip from special cash dispensers or telephone lines. The electronic cash can be transferred between individuals' cards, using a special "wallet" that resembles a pocket calculator.

Domestic media reports that Mondex was poised to set up in Japan as early as June, however, have proved overly optimistic, and one industry source said several Japanese banks which had considered taking part were backing away.
Some critics worry that rivalry between MITI and MPT could hamper Japan's electronic cash efforts, while others argue that Japanese efforts to develop its own systems are misguided.

"There is a need for firms from the financial, telecommunications and information sectors to link up, and it is not viable to envisage a single-country market," said an article in financial daily Nihon Keizai Shimbun.
"Shouldn't Japan emphasise, not developing its own system but removing legal and regulatory barriers...to introducing U.S. and European systems?" the paper said.

Japanese financial and monetary authorities, meanwhile, like their counterparts abroad, are pondering the implications of electronic money for the legal system and monetary policy. Concerns include money laundering and counterfeiting, and the possible privatisation of the issue of money.

A Finance Ministry study group aims to make its first report next spring. "When relevant laws were written, they did not envisage electronic money, so there is a question as to how far they apply," the Finance Ministry official said.
The Bank of Japan appears to be in no rush to utter official pronouncements.

"Official statements now might cool off the innovation process," said a financial source. "If electronic money spreads widely and develops into something equivalent to legal tender, then the central bank would have to comment, but I don't think it will spread so easily." ($1=110 yen)
